content.title: What Is Nowruz? When Is Nowruz in 2026?
content.text: Spring is finally here, which means it’s time for Nowruz! The holiday celebrates the start of the season and shares similar traditions to Easter, Passover and even Christmas. Learn all about the festivity and fun of Nowruz and get inspired to get festive.Related: What Is the March Birth Flower? Celebrate March Birthdays With This Beautiful Bloom Table of ContentsWhat Is Nowruz?When Is Nowruz 2026?How Long Do People Celebrate Nowruz?Which Countries Celebrate Nowruz?Is Nowruz a Holy or Religious Day? Nowruz is the Iranian (or Persian) New Year. Historically, it was observed mostly by Iranians and those of Persian descent; however, it is now celebrated by many cultures worldwide. 🎬 SIGN UP for Parade’s Daily newsletter to get the latest pop culture news & celebrity interviews delivered right to your inbox. 🎬 When Is Nowruz 2026? Nowruz 2026 is on Friday, March 20. Nowruz falls on the vernal equinox (first day of spring) each year. In other years, it can fall on March 20 or March 21. How Long Do People Celebrate Nowruz? The length of Nowruz celebrations can vary by region. It lasts 13 days in Iran.Related: 35 Spring Appetizers That Work for Every Kind of Celebratory Occasion Which Countries Celebrate Nowruz? Photo by Mizina from Getty Images/Canva Nowruz is a mostly secular holiday in Iran, as well as in Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, India, Iraq, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Is Nowruz a Holy or Religious Day? Nowruz is generally a secular holiday, but some religions, including Zoroastrianism and the Baháʼí Faith, as well as some Muslims, consider it a holy day.Related: April Showers Bring May Flowers—And the 135 Best Spring Instagram Captions Which Religion Celebrates Nowruz? Zoroastrians, Baháʼís and some Muslims celebrate Nowruz as a holy day. That said, Nowruz is widely considered a non-religious holiday. Nowruz History and Origins According to National Geographic, Nowruz stems from a religious holiday in Zoroastrianism dating back close to 3,000 years in Persia (now Iran), in which the coming of spring was celebrated as a triumph of good over evil. The holiday now extends into several different faiths and areas of the world. How to Celebrate Nowruz and the Persian New Year One of the biggest Nowruz traditions is probably one you’ve observed before: spring cleaning! Cleaning and “shaking the house” are common customs ahead of Nowruz. In more seasonal celebrations of spring, collecting flowers (especially tulips and hyacinths) and visiting with loved ones are all popular ways to mark the special day. Related: What Is Holi? Everything to Know About Holi, the Hindu Festival of Colors Nowruz Activities and Traditions Photo by rimmabondarenko/Canva Nowruz traditions vary from country to country and family to family, but the most common are: Amu Nowruz, Hajji Firuz and Kampirak Similar to Santa Claus, Amu Nowruz (often depicted with a long white or silver beard) and Hajji Firuz (who usually wears red, plays the tambourine, and is at least partially covered in soot) appear during Nowruz in Iran to greet children and often distribute gifts. Hajji Firuz has come under criticism for depicting blackface. In Afghanistan, Kampirak is a bearded man who wears brightly colored outfits and distributes charitable gifts for Nowruz. Khoncha In the Republic of Azerbaijan, one special Nowruz tradition is Khoncha, in which a table is set with seven dishes, and a large silver or copper tray is displayed. The tray has sprouting wheat and dyed eggs for every guest around it.Related: 130 Ways to Celebrate and Welcome the First Day of Spring Haft Mēwa In Afghanistan, Haft Mēwa is a type of compote made from seven dried fruits and nuts soaked in syrup. It often serves as a token of good luck for the new year. The individual types of nuts and fruit can vary, but usually include treats like raisins (yellow and black), dried apples, dried apricots, walnuts, pistachios, Persian olives, prunes, almonds or hazelnuts. Haft-sin At the precise moment of the vernal equinox, loved ones gather at a Haft-sin table, which is typically set in advance. The Haft-sin table traditionally has seven dishes starting with the Farsi letter sin (س). Translated, these dishes often include sprouts (typically lentil, wheat, barley or mung bean), apples, garlic, Persian olives, garlic, sumac and samanu (wheat germ pudding) and vinegar. There are also painted and dyed eggs, mirrors, water bowls, goldfish, coins, flowers, candles, candy and other festive symbols on the table as well. What Is Charshanbe Suri and How Is It Celebrated? Photo by Chinarius from Getty Images/Canva The evening of the final Wednesday before Nowruz is called Charshanbe Suri. The celebration (which translates to “Festive Wednesday”) often includes fireworks and bonfires. In Iran, celebrants often go door to door banging spoons in exchange for candy and packaged desserts, similar to trick-or-treating on Halloween (complete with costumes for some!). In the Republic of Azerbaijan, the festivities typically take place on Tuesdays every four weeks before Nowruz. What Is Sizdah Bedar? Sizdah Bedar is an outdoor festival to mark the 13th and final day of Nowruz. It’s often recognized with picnics and pranks.
